https://www.ft.com/content/ee5b23b3-89b3.summary: South Korean conglomerate hopes to replicate success with semiconductors across its sprawling portfolio of businesses
https://www.ft.com/content/ee5b23b3-89b3.author: Song Jung-a
https://www.ft.com/content/ee5b23b3-89b3.lead_paragraph: After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.
paragraphs: After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.

In the past year, the South Korean conglomerate has taken steps to try to become a one-stop provider of AI infrastructure. It has invested $1bn in a KKR- and Nvidia-backed data centre operator, acquired a European cooling systems maker and signed a partnership with OpenAI to develop AI infrastructure.

The group’s hope is to be able to offer a service in which it can build data centres through its construction arm, operate them through its IT services unit and provide energy storage systems through its battery maker, in addition to supplying memory chips.

“Moving forward, Samsung is poised to expand its role from a traditional hardware component supplier to an active architect of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem,” it said following its $1bn investment in Helix Digital Infrastructure in September.
Samsung is betting that its future in the AI boom lies beyond semiconductors, a highly lucrative but also highly cyclical industry.

While best known for Samsung Electronics — the manufacturing juggernaut that makes chips, Galaxy smartphones and household appliances — Samsung Group is a vast conglomerate with businesses as wide-ranging as insurance and security services.

Many of them started as internal units to serve the conglomerate and still count Samsung as their primary customer, but the group hopes some of the subsidiaries can expand to external clients as AI demand takes hold.

Samsung SDS, which began as an in-house IT services provider and operates data centres mostly to support the group, is in early-stage talks with Anthropic and OpenAI to potentially sign them on as tenants. Analysts expect the company to generate annual data centre revenue of Won6.6tn ($4.9bn) by 2031, roughly six times current levels.
Last year, Samsung signed a partnership with OpenAI to supply advanced memory chips to the company’s Stargate data centre initiative.

The agreement included Samsung SDS collaborating with OpenAI on designing, developing and operating data centres. Construction arm Samsung C&T and shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries also said they would work with the US tech company on developing floating data centres.

Morgan Stanley said in a recent report that Samsung SDS was well positioned to benefit from a surge in data centre construction, a trend reinforced by governments around the world passing laws requiring information to be stored domestically.

McKinsey estimates global data centre capacity demand could almost triple by 2030, with AI workloads accounting for about 70 per cent of the total. Meeting AI computing needs alone could require $5.2tn in capital expenditure.

“Samsung has an opportunity to provide a total solution,” said Joungho Kim, a professor of electrical engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. “US Big Tech companies are strong in AI and software, but they rely heavily on external suppliers for hardware.”
However, recent tech earnings have sparked investor concerns about the astronomical sums being spent on AI infrastructure and whether future demand will justify the cost.
Electoral victories of Democratic candidates in the US who pledged to halt data centre construction in their states have added to worries of regulatory pushback.
But Sanjeev Rana, head of Korea research at CLSA, said that while there would be “ups and downs” in the market, the spending was “structural”.
“In several years [and] decades, we are going to see huge investments in AI data centre-related products,” he said.
For Samsung, the challenge is bringing together disparate parts of its business empire.
Until 2017, the conglomerate had a Future Strategy Office responsible for group-wide decisions, but it was dismantled following a political corruption scandal involving its leadership.
Since then, Samsung has relied on so-called co-ordination bodies that are more lightly staffed, have fewer resources and are split based on business lines.
Analysts said the lack of a central decision-making body could complicate efforts to pursue more ambitious AI infrastructure projects that require close co-operation.
“Samsung has a broad range of capabilities, but it has been relatively weak at bringing them together [into an integrated offering],” said Peter Lee, an analyst at Citi.
There are also questions about experience serving external customers at scale as several subsidiaries remain heavily dependent on Samsung for work.
Rana said the group’s more immediate opportunity was in designing the systems inside data centres rather than operating the facilities themselves.
Samsung already supplies a range of components used in AI infrastructure including high-bandwidth memory chips, advanced packaging substrates for semiconductors and backup battery units for servers.

“Improving and extending the advantages in components will serve it better. And these are high-margin businesses,” said Rana. “Owning or operating data centres, I am not sure actually that will play to their strengths.”

https://www.ft.com/content/a3430f0d-0080.lead_paragraph: Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.
paragraphs: Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.
Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.
Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”
Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.
Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.
“Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.
Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.
A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.
However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.

Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.

Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”

Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.

Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.

“Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.

Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.

A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.

However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.

https://www.ft.com/content/5168b3e9-75d0.lead_paragraph: KPMG has carried out its first AI-based audit of a UK-listed company, saying the technology asked better questions than its own accountants about aspects of its client’s finances and dug deeper into some issues.
paragraphs: KPMG has carried out its first AI-based audit of a UK-listed company, saying the technology asked better questions than its own accountants about aspects of its client’s finances and dug deeper into some issues.

The Big Four firm this year deployed more than 100 AI agents to review the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, running the experiment parallel to a conventional audit by its accountants.
In several cases “the AI was able to go so much deeper” than the regular audit team, said Cath Burnet, KPMG’s UK head of audit, adding that in some situations it had asked “better questions”.
But in one area of the audit, a human had to intervene after an AI agent failed to match a set of regulations to the company’s documents, she added.

The project underlines AI’s potential to disrupt the sector by allowing accounts to be checked more quickly and cheaply even as regulators raise concerns about the risks associated with relying on artificial intelligence.
Audit firms have traditionally billed clients for large teams of junior accountants doing labour-intensive work, supervised by a small number of senior staff.
KPMG acknowledged there were “clear time-saving opportunities” from AI-based audits but declined to say whether this would in turn reduce fees.
KPMG International has itself negotiated lower fees from its auditor by arguing that AI will make the work cheaper.
Rival Big Four accounting firm PwC has also run several “parallel audit” projects to test AI extensively without relying on it, said Andy Hammond, the firm’s global assurance leader.
Auditors had previously used AI to help perform specific audit tasks, but until now the technology had not been used across all phases of a large UK audit.
In KPMG’s experiment, codenamed Project Exponential, agents deployed on different parts of the audit worked autonomously with each other and were able to suggest next steps.
AI agents had gathered data and analysed and documented it before forming draft conclusions and observations for the audit.
A team built the agents in four months and then had an audit partner “sign off” the experimental audit, which was not relied on by KPMG when it formally signed off on the company’s accounts.

KPMG declined to disclose the exact size of the team used in its AI-based audit but said that two partners and one director had worked with senior managers and junior staff building and running the agents.
The Project Exponential team had a “different shape and size” to a traditional audit, Burnet said, but human involvement had remained “critical”.

Staff set the agents’ objectives, supplied information about the company’s business and previous audits, checked the agents’ work periodically and challenged their conclusions before finalising the audit opinion.
The project will be expanded to up to 20 larger audits and KPMG hopes to eventually offer AI-based audits to its clients.

But the required technology was not yet available at the scale needed to run thousands of audits, Burnet said. Some companies may prefer not to use the service, and few currently had “clean” enough data for AI agents to work with, she added.
The rapid adoption of AI has sparked concerns about whether auditors can adequately oversee work carried out by machines.

The UK accounting regulator, the Financial Reporting Council, warned this week that using AI could pose a “distinct threat” to auditors’ integrity and independence if they used insights from AI agents to advise their clients. Auditors are restricted from providing advisory services to audit clients.

“Whatever technology a firm uses, the auditor remains accountable,” said Mark Babington, executive director of regulatory standards at the FRC. “Auditors need to be able to explain how they used it, challenge its outputs and stand behind the evidence.”

A report from the Centre for Public Interest Audit, a policy and research group for large audit firms, found last month that 23 per cent of company audit committee chairs, who appoint and oversee auditors, had “limited” confidence in AI.

Concerns included the risk of auditors becoming over-reliant on AI, weakening their scepticism, as well as data security and potential “hallucinations”, where the technology gives false, misleading or fabricated information.

Burnet said KPMG’s system provided “full visibility and full traceability” of the AI agents’ work, recording their interactions with documents down to individual characters and timestamps. KPMG gave the FRC a high-level overview of its experiment.

https://www.ft.com/content/08086201-6359.title: SoftBank regrets ‘mistake’ of not backing Anthropic, says Masayoshi Son
https://www.ft.com/content/08086201-6359.summary: Japanese tech group had already started to put money into arch-rival OpenAI
https://www.ft.com/content/08086201-6359.author: David Keohane and Madhumita Murgia
https://www.ft.com/content/08086201-6359.lead_paragraph: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has said he regrets not investing in Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, describing it as a mistake to pass up the chance to back the AI lab because he had already started to put money into its rival OpenAI.
paragraphs: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has said he regrets not investing in Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, describing it as a mistake to pass up the chance to back the AI lab because he had already started to put money into its rival OpenAI.

His comments come after OpenAI slashed its fundraising target by $10bn last month in its ongoing funding round, a deal overshadowed by an AI sell-off in the public markets and Anthropic’s plan to list this week at a target valuation of up to $1.4tn.

“We did have meetings [about investing in Anthropic]. But by that point, we had already decided to invest in OpenAI, and had already started doing so. So in that sense, there was a reluctance to pursue it further,” Son said at a Nikkei event on the Future of AI in Tokyo on Wednesday.
“This is an example of one of my mistakes,” Son said, describing the situation as like being unable to back “multiple horses” in the same race.
“When I met [Anthropic chief Dario Amodei] in person, I thought he was an incredible guy. I wish I’d invested back then,” Son added.
SoftBank has previously suggested that it had the opportunity to invest in Anthropic in 2023.
Anthropic’s rush to list this week is in stark contrast to OpenAI, which has delayed its own IPO until at least next year due to safety concerns surrounding the technology.
OpenAI last month cut its funding target by $10bn and is now seeking a $20bn round at a $1.25tn valuation, down from a potential $1.4tn valuation target in September.

SoftBank has already ploughed close to $65bn into the ChatGPT maker and is expected to participate in OpenAI’s latest funding round. A fundraising at a higher valuation would enable SoftBank to raise the value of its OpenAI stake on its own balance sheet.

SoftBank’s share price was up 3.1 per cent on Wednesday but is still down about 60 per cent since June as investors have increasingly questioned both the company’s own exposure to AI and the sector more broadly.
Son’s all-in strategy drove shares higher during the AI boom but has magnified the impact now that sentiment has turned, with many of SoftBank’s companies dependent on each other and OpenAI demand.

The Democrats’ crushing victory in the US midterm elections underlined the political risks surrounding SoftBank’s plans for large data centre developments in states such as Texas. The value of other major holdings has also fallen sharply, with UK chip designer Arm also down about 60 per cent since June.
